prime.problem: The flat MLP glues all 8 context characters into one long vector and squashes them in a single hidden layer. Everything is mixed in one step, and that first layer grows every time you widen the window.
prime.fits: It builds on the block_size-8 flat baseline (val 2.027) from the previous card. The architecture stays an MLP; only the wiring changes, so the context is fused gradually over several levels.
expect: fusion node (glue two children → Linear → BatchNorm → tanh)
weights shared across positions within a level
dilated causal convolution as a fast implementation
prime.goal: Draw the tree for any 8-character context, label every level's receptive field, and explain why a convolution computes the same model rather than a different one.

attend: Why does fusing two characters at a time mean the receptive field doubles per level, rather than growing by 2 each level?
Level 1 handles 4 pairs with one weight matrix. What does that sharing buy, and what does it assume about the pairs?
At about 22K parameters the tree only tied the flat net. Which later change made the tree pull ahead?
If block_size went from 8 to 16, what would the flat net's first layer and the tree each have to add?
In what sense are dilated causal convolutions "only an implementation detail", and what do they save?

must: each node fuses exactly 2 children → nodes halve at every level (8 → 4 → 2 → 1) → a level-L node sees 2L characters → 3 levels for block_size 8, and one more level per doubling of context

every node in a level uses the same Linear weights → level 1 stores 20 × 68 = 1,360 weights but applies them 4 times → the tree's cost grows with log<sub>2</sub> of the context, while the flat first layer grows linearly (6,000 → 16,000 → 32,000 weights at block_size 3 → 8 → 16)

the tree is a fixed pattern of "glue two neighbours, apply a shared layer" → sliding that pattern along a whole name is a convolution → dilated causal convolutions compute the same nodes for all positions at once and reuse overlapping ones (56 computed vs 34 distinct for diondre) → same model, only faster

wiring alone doesn't guarantee a win → at equal parameters (22,097 flat vs 22,397 tree) val was 2.027 vs 2.029 (then 2.022 after the BatchNorm fix) → the tree's advantage in the lecture shows up only when it is scaled up (76,579 params, val 1.9937)
elevated: the tree pairs fixed positions (1+2, 3+4, …) → which characters meet first is baked into the architecture → a pattern split across a pair boundary (e.g. positions 2 and 3) only meets at level 2
reference: the paper's figure has 4 levels (receptive field 16), with dilations 1, 2, 4, 8
WaveNet paper: van den Oord et al. 2016, arXiv 1609.03499

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the tree for the context .diondre and label every level's receptive field. Then, in 3–4 sentences, explain why this wiring is different from the flat MLP and why a dilated convolution doesn't change it.
checklist: 8 leaves (embeddings), then 4, 2 and 1 fusion nodes, each gluing two children and applying Linear → BatchNorm → tanh
receptive field 2, 4, 8 (= 2<sup>L</sup>); one extra level per doubling of context
one weight matrix per level, shared by every node in it
the flat MLP mixes all 8 characters in its first layer, and that layer grows linearly with block_size
a dilated causal convolution computes the same tree at every position at once and reuses shared nodes: it's faster, not a different model

retrieve.q: Explain what "fusing context slowly" means in the tree, compared with how the flat MLP handles the same 8 characters.
answer: flat: all 8 embeddings concatenated (80 numbers) into one hidden layer at once
tree: fuse neighbouring pairs, then pairs of pairs, then the two halves
each node only ever combines two inputs, so the context is built up over 3 levels

retrieve.q: Walk the context .diondre through the tree: what does each level's nodes cover, and what shape does the batch of 4 have after each regrouping?
answer: level 1: .d, io, nd, re; (4,8,10) → (4,4,20) → Linear → (4,4,n_hidden)
level 2: .dio, ndre; (4,2,2·n_hidden) → (4,2,n_hidden)
level 3: .diondre; (4,2·n_hidden) → (4,n_hidden) → output Linear → (4,27) logits

retrieve.q: You want 16 characters of context. Compare what the flat net (200 hidden) and the tree (n_hidden 68) must add, and name one thing the tree gives up for its cheaper growth.
answer: flat: the first layer goes from 80 × 200 = 16,000 to 160 × 200 = 32,000 weights
tree: one more level, 136 × 68 + 136 = 9,384 params
the tree gives up freedom: which characters meet first is fixed, and every pair must share one set of weights

retrieve.q: Someone says "WaveNet is a convolutional net, so the lecture's MLP tree isn't really WaveNet." What's right and wrong about that?
answer: the model (the black tree in the figure) is the same as the lecture's hierarchical MLP
the convolution is how you compute that tree for every position of a sequence at once, reusing overlapping nodes
what the lecture really leaves out is gated activations and residual and skip connections

compare.q: Flat MLP with block_size 8 vs the tree at the same ~22K parameters: what is fundamentally different, which design choice causes it, and why didn't the tree win straight away?
answer: same data, same embeddings, similar budget (22,097 vs 22,397)
flat mixes all 80 numbers in one layer; the tree mixes two at a time with shared weights per level
the val losses tied (2.027 vs 2.029); a BatchNorm bug and no tuning held the tree back
flat fails by growing linearly and crushing everything early; the tree fails if its fixed pairing splits a pattern that matters

compare.q: This card's tree vs the convolution view of it: which one is the model and which is the computation strategy? When would you notice the difference?
answer: the tree defines what gets computed; the convolution defines how, for all positions at once
the Python loop recomputes shared nodes (56 computed vs 34 distinct for diondre's 8 rows); a convolution doesn't
you'd notice it in speed on long sequences, never in the loss

compare.q: Bengio's 2003 MLP concatenates the context embeddings into one hidden layer. What does the tree keep from it, and what does it change?
answer: keeps: a learned embedding per character and an MLP predicting the next one
changes: the concatenation happens in pairs over several levels instead of all at once
the Bengio layout's first layer scales with context length; the tree's scales with log<sub>2</sub> of it

predict.q: Keep the lecture's tree, but set block_size to 6 instead of 8. What goes wrong when you fuse pairs, and what are two ways to fix it?
predict.answer: 6 → 3 → then 3 nodes can't be split into pairs, so the third level breaks (in code, view fails or the shapes stop matching). Fixes: pad the context to a power of two (8), or fuse in groups of 3 at one level (6 → 2 → 1 with a FlattenConsecutive(3) and a FlattenConsecutive(2)). The pairwise tree quietly assumes the context length is 2L.

apply.task: Extend your drawing to block_size 16 (4 levels, like the paper's figure). Count the fusion nodes per example, then compute the parameter count of the 4-level tree at n_embd 10, n_hidden 68, and of a flat MLP with 200 hidden units on the same 16 characters.
apply.done: You get 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 fusion nodes, 22,397 + 9,384 = 31,781 parameters for the tree, and 270 + 160 × 200 + 400 + 5,427 = 38,097 for the flat net.
apply.hint: A new level adds one Linear of (2 × 68) × 68 weights plus BatchNorm's γ and β (2 × 68). In the flat net, only the first layer changes: 16 × 10 = 160 inputs.
